questions.question_text: Utility is subjective because:
options: It is fixed for all goods
It varies from person to person, place and time
It is measured by the government
questions.explanation: The same good gives different satisfaction to different people.

questions.question_text: Utility differs from usefulness in that utility:
options: Is the want-satisfying power of a good, whether or not the good is beneficial
questions.explanation: A cigarette has utility for a smoker though it is not useful.

questions.question_text: Utility has no moral meaning because:
options: A good has utility if it satisfies a want, regardless of whether the want is desirable
questions.explanation: Liquor has utility for a drinker even though it is harmful.

questions.question_text: Which is NOT one of Marshall's forms of utility?
questions.explanation: Form, place, time, service and possession utility.

questions.question_text: The cardinal utility approach assumes utility:
options: Can be measured in numbers called utils
questions.explanation: It is the basis of Marshall's marginal utility analysis.

questions.question_text: The ordinal utility approach assumes utility:
options: Can only be ranked in order of preference
questions.explanation: Hicks and Allen: consumers can rank bundles as first, second, third.

questions.question_text: Which pair is correct?
options: Cardinal – Marshall; Ordinal – Hicks and Allen
questions.explanation: Cardinal approach is Marshall's; ordinal is Hicks and Allen's.

questions.question_text: The ordinal approach is considered more realistic because it:
options: Needs only ranking and not a constant MU of money
questions.explanation: Consumers can rank preferences but cannot measure satisfaction exactly.

questions.question_text: Total utility (TU) is:
options: The sum of marginal utilities, TU = ΣMU
The utility of the last unit
questions.explanation: It is the total satisfaction from all units consumed.

questions.question_text: Marginal utility is:
options: The total utility of all units
ΔTU/ΔQ – the addition to TU from one more unit
questions.explanation: MUn = TUn − TUn−1.

questions.question_text: Average utility is calculated as:
questions.explanation: AU = total utility divided by number of units.

questions.question_text: When MU is positive but falling, TU:
questions.explanation: Each extra unit still adds to TU but by less.

questions.question_text: When MU is zero, TU is:
questions.explanation: This is the point of satiety.

questions.question_text: The point of satiety is where:
options: MU is zero and TU is maximum
questions.explanation: The consumer is fully satisfied with no further gain.

questions.question_text: Disutility means:
options: Negative marginal utility – dissatisfaction from additional consumption
questions.explanation: Consuming beyond satiety reduces total satisfaction.

questions.question_text: When MU is negative, TU:
questions.explanation: Additional units reduce total satisfaction.

questions.question_text: If TU = 10, 18, 24, 28, 30, the MU of the units is:
If MU = 40, 30, 20, 10, 0, the TU of the five units is:
questions.explanation: TU is the running sum of MU.

questions.question_text: TU from 4 units is 68 and from 5 units is 68. The MU of the fifth unit is:
questions.explanation: The change in TU is 68 − 68 = 0.

questions.question_text: The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility states that as more units are consumed, MU of each additional unit:
questions.explanation: Each successive unit satisfies a less urgent want.

questions.question_text: The law of DMU is credited to:
questions.explanation: It is also known as Gossen's First Law.

questions.question_text: A schedule showing TU 30, 50, 62, 68 for 1 to 4 units illustrates DMU because:
questions.explanation: Falling MU as consumption rises is the law of DMU.

questions.question_text: In a DMU diagram, the MU curve:
options: Slopes downward from left to right
questions.explanation: MU falls as quantity increases.

questions.question_text: An assumption of the law of DMU is:
options: Units consumed are of varying size
questions.explanation: Other things like tastes, income and habits are constant.

questions.question_text: "Homogeneous units" matter in DMU because:
options: They make goods identical, so MU change is due only to quantity consumed
questions.explanation: If units differed in quality or size, MU might not diminish.

questions.question_text: MU diminishes because:
options: Successive units satisfy less intense wants
questions.explanation: The most urgent want is satisfied first.

questions.question_text: Which is an exception to the law of DMU?
options: Collection of rare stamps or coins
questions.explanation: Hobbies and collections can give increasing MU.

questions.question_text: About the law of DMU and money:
options: It is said not to apply to misers whose desire for money increases with wealth
It does not apply to goods
questions.explanation: Misers are traditionally cited as an exception.

questions.question_text: For a collection hobby the law of DMU:
options: May not apply as each additional item can raise satisfaction
questions.explanation: The collector's MU may rise as the collection nears completion.

questions.question_text: The diamond–water paradox arises because water has:
options: High total utility but low marginal utility due to abundance, while diamonds are the opposite
questions.explanation: Price reflects marginal utility, not total utility.

questions.question_text: The law of DMU is the basis of the law of demand because:
options: Consumers pay more for each extra unit
Consumers are willing to pay less for extra units as MU falls
questions.explanation: Falling MU means lower willingness to pay, so demand slopes down.

questions.question_text: Progressive taxation is supported by DMU because:
options: MU of money rises with income
MU of money falls as income rises, so the rich lose less satisfaction from a rupee of tax
questions.explanation: Taxing higher incomes at higher rates equalises sacrifice.

questions.question_text: An importance of the law of DMU is that it:
options: Explains downward-sloping demand and the diamond–water paradox
questions.explanation: It underlies several consumer theories.

questions.question_text: A limitation of the law of DMU is that it:
options: Assumes utility is measurable and holds only under given assumptions
questions.explanation: Cardinal measurement and ceteris paribus restrict its validity.

questions.question_text: The Law of Equi-Marginal Utility says a consumer maximises satisfaction when:
options: MU per rupee spent is equal across goods
questions.explanation: MUx/Px = MUy/Py = MUm.

questions.question_text: An assumption of the law of equi-marginal utility is:
options: Limited income and independent utilities of goods
questions.explanation: Plus rationality, cardinal utility and constant MU of money.

questions.question_text: If a schedule shows MUx/Px equal to MUy/Py after spending all income, the consumer is:
questions.explanation: Equal marginal utility per rupee means no gain from reallocating.

questions.question_text: If MUx/Px > MUy/Py, the consumer should:
options: Buy more Y and less X
Buy more X and less Y
questions.explanation: He gains by shifting spending to X until ratios are equal.

questions.question_text: MUx = 20, Px = 4, MUy = 18, Py = 3. The consumer should buy more of:
questions.explanation: MUx/Px = 5 and MUy/Py = 6, so Y gives more utility per rupee.

questions.question_text: The law of equi-marginal utility applies to:
options: Consumption, production, public finance and saving decisions
questions.explanation: Any allocation of limited resources among competing uses.

questions.question_text: Consumer surplus is the difference between:
options: What a consumer is willing to pay and what he actually pays
questions.explanation: It is the extra satisfaction a buyer gets.

questions.question_text: The concept of consumer surplus was introduced by:
questions.explanation: Marshall developed it from Dupuit's idea.

questions.question_text: Consumer surplus equals:
questions.explanation: Total utility minus actual payment.

questions.question_text: Willingness to pay Rs. 50 for a book priced Rs. 35 gives a consumer surplus of:
In a schedule, consumer surplus for a unit is:
options: Value placed on the unit minus the price
questions.explanation: Add these gains across units to get total CS.

questions.question_text: In a demand diagram, consumer surplus is the area:
options: Between the demand curve and the price line
questions.explanation: The triangle between demand and the market price.

questions.question_text: A limitation of consumer surplus is that:
options: It is valid for all goods
Utility is not measurable and MU of money is not constant
questions.explanation: These weaken precise measurement.

questions.question_text: An importance of consumer surplus is that it:
options: Shows the gain from exchange and helps in taxation and welfare analysis
questions.explanation: It measures benefits consumers get above what they pay.

questions.question_text: Consumer surplus cannot be measured accurately because:
options: Utility cannot be measured exactly and willingness to pay is subjective
questions.explanation: Subjective valuations and changing MU of money prevent precision.

questions.question_text: An indifference curve shows:
options: Combinations of two goods giving the same satisfaction
questions.explanation: The consumer is indifferent between all points.

questions.question_text: The indifference curve approach was developed by:
questions.explanation: Introduced by Edgeworth, developed by Hicks and Allen (1934).

questions.question_text: An indifference schedule lists:
options: Combinations of two goods that give equal satisfaction
questions.explanation: E.g. 1 apple + 12 oranges, 2 + 8 etc., all equally satisfying.

questions.question_text: An indifference map is:
options: A set of indifference curves, with higher curves showing higher satisfaction
questions.explanation: It represents the consumer's whole preference ordering.

questions.question_text: MRS is the rate at which a consumer is willing to:
options: Give up units of one good for an additional unit of another, keeping satisfaction constant
questions.explanation: MRSxy = −ΔY/ΔX.

questions.question_text: MRS diminishes because:
options: As more X is held, X becomes less valuable relative to Y
questions.explanation: The consumer is willing to give up less Y for each extra X.

questions.question_text: MRSxy equals:
questions.explanation: The ratio of marginal utilities.

questions.question_text: The IC slopes downward because:
options: More of one good must be offset by less of the other to keep satisfaction constant
questions.explanation: If both increased, satisfaction would also rise.

questions.question_text: The IC is convex to the origin because of:
questions.explanation: The slope flattens as more X is substituted for Y.

questions.question_text: Two ICs cannot intersect because it would:
options: Violate consistency and transitivity of preferences
questions.explanation: The intersection point would imply two satisfaction levels.

questions.question_text: A higher IC represents higher satisfaction because it has:
options: More of at least one good
questions.explanation: By non-satiation, more is preferred to less.

questions.question_text: An IC does not touch either axis because:
questions.explanation: Touching an axis would mean consuming only one good.

questions.question_text: Which is an assumption of IC analysis?
questions.explanation: Also ordinal utility, non-satiation and diminishing MRS.

questions.question_text: For perfect substitutes the IC is:
options: A straight line with constant MRS
questions.explanation: The consumer substitutes at a constant rate.

questions.question_text: For perfect complements the IC is:
options: L-shaped, e.g. left and right shoes
questions.explanation: Goods are consumed in a fixed proportion.

questions.question_text: For a neutral good the IC is:
options: A straight line parallel to an axis
questions.explanation: Changing the quantity of a neutral good does not change satisfaction.

questions.question_text: A budget line shows:
options: Combinations of two goods the consumer can buy with given income and prices
questions.explanation: It is the boundary of affordable bundles.

questions.question_text: The equation of the budget line is:
questions.explanation: Total expenditure equals income.

questions.question_text: Income Rs. 200, Px = 10, Py = 20. The X-axis and Y-axis intercepts are:
questions.explanation: M/Px = 20 and M/Py = 10.

questions.question_text: The slope of the budget line equals:
questions.explanation: It shows the relative price of X in terms of Y.

questions.question_text: A point inside the budget line means:
options: Affordable, but part of income is unspent
questions.explanation: The bundle costs less than income.

questions.question_text: A point outside the budget line means:
questions.explanation: It costs more than the consumer's income.

questions.question_text: When income rises with prices constant, the budget line:
questions.explanation: Both intercepts rise proportionally; slope is unchanged.

questions.question_text: When Px falls, the budget line:
questions.explanation: The X-intercept M/Px increases.

questions.question_text: When Py rises, the budget line:
questions.explanation: The Y-intercept M/Py decreases.

questions.question_text: If both prices fall by the same percentage, the budget line:
questions.explanation: Real income rises while the price ratio stays the same.

questions.question_text: Consumer equilibrium is a situation where the consumer:
options: Maximises satisfaction given income and prices with no tendency to change
questions.explanation: It is the optimum choice.

questions.question_text: For a single commodity, the equilibrium condition is:
options: MUx = Px (in terms of MU of money)
questions.explanation: Marginal utility equals price.

questions.question_text: For two commodities (cardinal approach), equilibrium requires:
questions.explanation: MU per rupee is equal across goods.

questions.question_text: With Rs. 10 and MU per rupee equal across goods after the last rupee is spent, the consumer is:
questions.explanation: No reallocation increases total utility.

questions.question_text: In the IC approach, equilibrium is where:
options: The budget line cuts an IC
The budget line is tangent to the highest attainable IC
questions.explanation: Slopes are equal at the tangency point.

questions.question_text: The first-order and second-order conditions are:
options: MRS = price ratio; IC convex to the origin
questions.explanation: Tangency (necessary) and diminishing MRS (sufficient).

questions.question_text: At the tangency point of the highest attainable IC and budget line:
questions.explanation: The slopes of IC and budget line are equal.

questions.question_text: The consumer is not in equilibrium where the budget line cuts an IC because:
options: He can move along the budget line to a higher IC
questions.explanation: A higher IC is attainable.

questions.question_text: A corner solution arises when:
options: The consumer spends all income on only one good
questions.explanation: It happens, e.g., with perfect substitutes when MRS never equals the price ratio.

questions.question_text: The income-consumption curve (ICC) is the locus of equilibrium points when:
questions.explanation: Each income level gives a new equilibrium.

questions.question_text: An Engel curve shows the relation between:
questions.explanation: It is derived from the ICC.

questions.question_text: For an inferior good the ICC:
questions.explanation: Consumption of the inferior good falls as income rises.

questions.question_text: The price-consumption curve (PCC) is the locus of equilibrium points when:
options: The price of one good changes, income and the other price constant
questions.explanation: Each price gives a new budget line and equilibrium.

questions.question_text: The demand curve is derived from the PCC by plotting:
options: Price of X against the quantity of X at each equilibrium
questions.explanation: This gives the downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.question_text: The price effect is the:
options: Total change in consumption due to a change in price
questions.explanation: It equals substitution effect plus income effect.

questions.question_text: Price effect equals:
questions.explanation: It splits into two components.

questions.question_text: The substitution effect is the change in consumption due to:
options: Change in relative price keeping real income constant
questions.explanation: It is always negative.

questions.question_text: The income effect is the change in consumption due to:
options: Change in real income resulting from a price change
questions.explanation: Positive for normal goods and negative for inferior goods.

questions.question_text: The income effect is negative for:
questions.explanation: Higher real income reduces the purchase of inferior goods.

questions.question_text: Giffen goods are:
options: Inferior goods whose demand falls when price falls
questions.explanation: The negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect.

questions.question_text: Giffen goods have upward-sloping demand because:
options: The income effect is negative and stronger than the substitution effect
questions.explanation: A price rise lowers real income so much that people buy more of the good.

questions.question_text: Cardinal equilibrium requires MUx/Px = MUy/Py, while ordinal equilibrium requires:
questions.explanation: Both conditions are equivalent since MRS = MUx/MUy.

questions.question_text: Income Rs. 120, Px = 6, Py = 4, MRS = 2. The price ratio is 1.5, so the consumer:
options: Should buy more Y and less X
Is not in equilibrium and should buy more X and less Y
questions.explanation: MRS (2) > Px/Py (1.5): he values X more than the market price implies.

questions.question_text: The Law of DMU deals with a single commodity, whereas the Law of Equi-Marginal Utility deals with:
options: Two or more commodities and income allocation
questions.explanation: DMU explains the fall in MU; equi-marginal utility explains optimal spending.

questions.question_text: When income doubles with prices constant, the budget line:
options: Shifts parallel outward, giving a new equilibrium on a higher IC
questions.explanation: The consumer moves along the ICC to a higher satisfaction level.
